title: The Name Beneath the Bell
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 3 of 10
content:
The bell under Lanternwell Square was not supposed to ring.

That was what Neri, the valley's oldest resident, told us as we knelt beside the spring. Neri had grey curls, a walking stick cut from dark wood, and the unsettling habit of noticing questions before people asked them.

“It hasn't sounded since the last lost traveler found their way,” they said.

“Lost traveler?” I repeated.

Neri looked at Maui. Maui suddenly became interested in examining a crack in the stone.

The crack had a sliver of blue-green moss growing along it. Maui prodded the edge with one finger.

"That stone is clearly losing an argument with the great Maui. I can settle it."

"Please don't," Neri said.

"It's a crack."

"It's the wall of a spring people drink from. Tamsin has been measuring it since the last hard rain."

At the edge of the square, Tamsin stood beside a bucket beneath a seep, checking two chalk marks. She called across that the crack hadn't widened and that she needed a date for the maintenance ledger, not a heroic demolition.

Maui looked wounded. "I've pulled entire islands out of the sea."

"Then fetching my ledger should be easy," Neri said.

The book was tiny. He carried it across the square as though it were a sacred mountain.

"Behold! An impossible feat of strength."

Nobody applauded except me. I laughed before I could stop myself. The sound helped; my key was still cold in my hand.

The spring had a life that continued whether I remembered anything or not: people tending it, people arguing over repairs, people arriving for water and leaving when they pleased. A place was not required to become a miracle just because I needed one.

Maui set the ledger where it wouldn't get wet. "If your name turns out to be magnificent, I claim partial credit."

"You haven't even heard it."

"Details. A proper legend leaves room for surprises."

“The valley does not take people,” Neri explained. “Doors open. Travelers choose. Sometimes someone arrives before they remember the road behind them.”

“Can the spring tell me who I was?”

“It can show what is attached to the key. Whether you wish to look is yours.”

I unwound the blue thread at my wrist. The brass key slid into my palm. There was a tiny notch near its teeth, shaped like a half-moon.

Neri unfolded a small cloth beside the spring and set it across the stone.

"People often imagine a spring like this gives answers," they said. "It doesn't speak in sentences. Sometimes it reflects something attached to the object you bring. Sometimes it shows nothing."

"What happens if I don't like what I see?"

"Then we stop."

Maui looked toward the water.

"Oh, good. A magical spring with rules," Maui said. "I was afraid this place was going to be boring."

"Not always," Neri said. "People can become desperate for an answer. I have seen them keep asking long after they were ready to listen."

I touched the half-moon notch in the key.

"Would it hurt the spring to try?"

"No. But it might hurt you to see something before you're ready. That is why I'm explaining it first."

I thought about the way my mind had gone blank when I reached for a name. I had spent every night since the beach feeling that absence like a missing tooth. Part of me wanted to thrust the key into the water and demand that the whole world give me back whatever had been taken.

Another part wanted to keep walking and never ask again.

Neri said, "You could come back tomorrow."

Maui shifted his lantern to his other hand.

"Or next week. The spring isn't going anywhere."

"Are you sure?"

"Pretty sure. It would be difficult to move this much stone."

I laughed despite the tightness in my chest.

I looked at the spring again.

"I want to try now," I said.

Neri nodded, then stepped back.

Maui held the lantern while I approached the water. He did not reach for my hand. I was beginning to understand that his restraint was deliberate.

The moment the key touched the spring, a bell rang beneath the stones.

I saw a kitchen with a window full of rain. A table covered in papers. Someone telling me I would always be the dependable one. The memory flashed away before I could decide whether the voice had been loving or demanding.

Then came a word, clear as a pebble hitting the bottom of a well.

Jasper.

I stumbled. Maui caught my elbow only after I reached for him.

“That's my name,” I whispered.

Neri waited.

I said it again, testing the sound against the shape of myself. “Jasper.”

Maui tried it with exaggerated solemnity. “Jasper. Excellent name. Strong. Dramatic. Goes with heroic companions.”

The little tattoo on his chest caught his eye, pantomimed a bow, and made a grand flourish toward me.

"Don't encourage him," I warned.

"Encourage me? This is restraint. I'm capable of commissioning a fifty-foot statue for a name like that."

"You are not commissioning a statue."

"Forty feet, then. Incredible negotiation skills."

Neri made a sound that might have been a cough or a laugh. Maui bent dramatically at the waist, one broad hand across his chest. Then he straightened and said "Jasper" again, without an announcement surrounding it. His grin remained, but the word was mine and he seemed to know it.

Mini Maui pointed at the actual spring instead of the imaginary statue. That was probably the most useful advice either of them had given all morning.

“I'm standing right here.”

“Which proves my point.”

I laughed, and the sound broke something open that fear had kept shut.

For a long time I stood there listening to the ordinary water.

The bell had fallen silent. People were going about their business beyond the fountain: someone lifting a basket of bread, a pair of neighbors discussing a leaking roof, a child laughing as a paper lantern turned in the breeze. Nobody stopped what they were doing to insist I explain what the spring had shown.

I wondered how many of them had arrived by a door they didn't understand.

Neri watched my face.

"Will you write the name in the arrival book?" they asked.

I hesitated.

"What happens if I do?"

"It helps us address you correctly and return things you borrow. It doesn't mean you belong to the valley, and it doesn't give anyone authority over where you travel."

"Could I change it?"

"Of course."

I looked at the book on the nearby table. There were empty lines between names, not the kind of narrow crowded spaces that made a person feel as though they had to squeeze themselves to fit.

"Then I want to write it myself."

Neri handed me the pen.

My first attempt left a blot of ink beside the J. My hand shook, and I hated it for shaking. I almost reached for a fresh page.

"Can I leave the blot?" I asked.

"It's your line."

I wrote the rest.

Jasper.

The letters weren't elegant. They were mine.

Maui leaned over the table.

"That looks very official."

"It's handwriting."

"Official handwriting."

I nudged him with my elbow.

Neri's registry had a second column I hadn't noticed. Beside the names were little marks showing whether a traveler wanted someone notified that they'd arrived.

"What does this symbol mean?" I asked.

"It means the person chose not to have a message sent."

Maui glanced at the page, then deliberately looked away when Neri moved it closer to me. He was trying; I could tell by the very serious expression he wore.

"Can I leave mine blank until I know who I might tell?" I asked.

"Yes," Neri said. "A name and an address are not the same thing."

It was a small distinction, but it loosened something in my chest. I had written Jasper without having to provide a history to justify it. I could decide later whether to contact the people behind the door, or whether to ask someone I trusted to help me do it.

Maui pointed to the wet ink. "What if you change your handwriting?"

"Then my name won't fall off."

"Excellent. I had been concerned."

I laughed. Neri slid the page beneath blotting paper and gave me a separate card for questions I wanted to ask before a future crossing. I wrote one: *Who can see my information?* The fact that I could ask that without being ungrateful for their help felt unexpectedly important.

When we left, the bell remained quiet. My name didn't need to make it ring for the day to matter.

He grinned, then grew unexpectedly quiet.

"Would you rather I didn't tell anyone what happened?" he asked.

I looked up.

"Why?"

"Because you might want to decide when people hear the story."

I thought about it. The name was good news; the glimpse of the rainy kitchen was something I wasn't ready to unpack in front of strangers.

"You can tell them I remembered my name. Not the picture I saw."

He nodded.

"Done."

It was a small agreement, made beside a fountain with somebody waiting to carry bread through the square. I had no idea yet how much I'd come to value it.

I closed the arrival book gently and handed the pen back.

The spring held no more pictures. I expected disappointment, but I felt a strange tenderness toward the one small thing it had given me.

“Does knowing your name help?” Maui asked as we crossed the square.

“Yes. No. Maybe.” I looked at the houses. “I don't know if I liked who I was.”

He stopped near a row of lanterns.

“Then don't decide that today.”

“What if I never remember?”

“Then you'll still be Jasper, if you want to be.”

I stared at him. People who called themselves heroes were supposed to tell you what came next. Maui, who clearly adored the sound of his own voice, had somehow left the important space empty.

“Is that all?” I asked.

“Nope. Now I'm going to brag about how I helped the most fascinating person on this coast discover a name. It'll take at least twenty minutes.”

“You didn't discover it. I did.”

He smiled, sharp and delighted.

“Exactly.”

That evening I took the brass key to the little room Neri had offered above the Lanternwell bakery. I wrote my name on a scrap of paper and pinned it beside the bed, not because I feared forgetting it again but because I liked being able to choose where it belonged.

Down below, Maui was telling someone a very inaccurate version of our morning.

I opened the window.

“You left out the part where you nearly fell in the spring!”

He looked up, grinning.

“Artistic license!”

For the first time, the name Jasper felt less like a missing label and more like an introduction.
